name: Kubernetes
summary: A distributed control system that exposes declarative resources through an API, persists cluster state, and uses controllers and schedulers to drive observed state toward desired state across nodes.

features.name: Declarative API resource model
features.description: Kubernetes represents workloads and cluster configuration as API objects with desired and observed state, exposed through the control plane and consumed by cluster components.
benefits: Provides a common, inspectable boundary for workload and infrastructure state
Allows clients and controllers to converge on API-described intent
costs: API versions, validation, and compatibility become system-wide constraints
An API object records intent but does not itself perform the requested work

features.name: Controller reconciliation loops
features.description: Kubernetes controllers watch relevant resources, enqueue work, and repeatedly reconcile observed cluster state toward the desired state represented by those resources.
benefits: Allows responsibilities to be split among specialized controllers
costs: Convergence depends on retries, event delivery, and idempotent handlers
Transient divergence is expected while reconciliation is in progress

lifecycle.notes: The fixed official documentation and source directly record controller work processing and reconciliation behavior for the cited revision.

features.name: etcd-backed cluster state
features.description: The Kubernetes API server uses a storage layer backed by etcd for persistent cluster state, while API-server code mediates serialization, resource operations, and storage access.
benefits: Provides a durable coordination substrate for API reads, writes, and watches
costs: Control-plane availability and latency depend on the storage path
Storage schema and consistency behavior constrain API evolution

features.name: Scheduler-based node placement
features.description: Kubernetes separates the decision to place a pending workload on a node from the node agent that runs it, allowing scheduling policies and node capabilities to participate in placement.
benefits: Makes placement a policy-driven control-plane decision
Supports heterogeneous nodes and resource constraints
costs: Placement quality depends on current cluster observations and policy configuration
A scheduling decision can become stale before execution

mathematical_views.question: How do controllers use observations and desired resource state to drive cluster state toward a target?
assumptions: Desired state is represented by API resources
Controllers can observe relevant state and perform idempotent actions
The system may remain temporarily divergent while work is queued or retried

lifecycle.notes: Candidate lifecycle model proposed from the cited controller documentation and source; temporary divergence and convergence are assumptions, not a proven guarantee for every workload.

mathematical_views.model: Typed resource graph with durable state
mathematical_views.question: How are API resources, ownership relationships, storage records, and node assignments connected?
assumptions: Resource kinds and references define typed graph nodes and edges
etcd-backed API state is treated as authoritative for the modeled control plane
The graph abstracts away implementation details of individual workloads

mathematical_views.question: How does a pending workload move through scheduling, binding, and node execution states?
assumptions: A workload has a pending state before a placement decision
Scheduler observations and node availability can change between decision and execution
The model does not claim that every workload reaches running state

benefits: Common API boundary for automation and independent controllers
costs: Schema, versioning, and admission behavior add coordination overhead

benefits: Resilience through retries and separation of control responsibilities
costs: Eventual convergence and duplicate work require idempotency and observability

benefits: Durable, shared control-plane state with watchable changes
costs: Storage health becomes a critical dependency for cluster management
Decisions can be constrained by stale observations and competing workloads
